https://www.dw.com/en/france-suspends-us.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NtoP Police have fired tear gas to break up demonstrations in several French cities since protests began Image: Fred Tanneau/AFP Advertisement France is suspending the use of stun grenades at student-led protests as people report allegations of police brutality at demonstrations that have widened over the weeks . "I am suspending their use in the high school student protests until the facts of the incident have been clarified," Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told RTL radio broadcaster on Wednesday. He emphasized that the suspension was "only for the high school student protests" and for "just long enough to understand what happened." What led to the focus on 'sting ball grenades?' Nunez announced the measure to curb growing anger after reports of serious injuries to teenage protesters drew public anger. On Monday, a 15-year-old lost his hand after picking up a particular type of police stun grenade, a sting ball grenade, that then detonated before he could throw it back. Last week, a 14-year-old student in northwest Paris was hit in the jaw as a tear gas canister was fired during protests. The officer was charged on Tuesday. Students' anger 'does not come from nowhere,' prime minister says Speaking later on Wednesday, French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said France could not remain "indifferent" to students' concerns and that the "anger of young people does not come from nowhere." "In the past, too many promises were not kept, quite simply because they were untenable," Lecornu said in a televised address. "What I ​want are concrete, quick and fully funded answers." Lecornu denied that security forces have "orders to confront" the protesters after scenes of violent clashes. He also promised the government would present its first decisions to respond to the crisis "at the end of October." AI-generated fake social media videos claiming to show police officials threatening protesters have only served to amplify the issue. The head of Paris police, Patrice Faure, on Wednesday explicitly rejected the contents of one widely-shared TikTok video claiming to show him threatening "indiscriminate" use of tear gas grenades and a risk of "even more amputations." He reminded those making the videos that they risked prosecution, urging them to "return to reason" while appealing to others "not to let yourselves be manipulated." Nunez said on Monday that 761 police officers or gendarmes had been wounded during the roughly three weeks of protests, as well as 215 students and 89 teaching staff. France students demand better schools To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video France summons Iran's ambassador over 'disinformation campaign' The French Foreign Ministry on Wednesday summoned Iran's ambassador to protest against a "disinformation campaign conducted by the Iranian authorities." The ambassador was told that "the misleading content disseminated online" by Iran's Foreign Ministry was "absolutely unacceptable." Iran had earlier summoned France's ambassador to complain of "violent treatment" against protesters and of "extensive human rights violations." This seemed a thinly veiled attempt to draw parallels between the unrest and the brutal government crackdown on anti-government protests in Iran this year, particularly in early January. The Norway-based NGO Iran Human Rights says it has identified 4,219 people killed in those protests, and warned the real tally is likely far higher. The demonstrations are also taking place at a difficult time for the French government as it tries to rein in its debts while facing demands to spend more on public services — all just a few months before presidential elections where incumbent Emmanuel Macron will not be eligible to run. How long have students been protesting in France? Protests first began mid-September in the Paris region after students began mobilizing against perceived inequalities in the education system. From the outset, pupils said teaching, facilities and opportunities for advancement weren't as good for students in disadvantaged neighborhoods — despite the promise of France's national motto of "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity." Demonstrations then spread to all parts of the country, including smaller towns with high schools. On Tuesday, trade unions joined student protests. The Interior Ministry said nearly 256,000 people took part in protests nationwide on Tuesday. Protests turned violent in Paris, where small groups of protesters clashed with riot officers at a city square toward the end. More than 6,500 people have been arrested over the course of the last two weeks, most of them minors. China is lashing out at the new conservative Japanese PM Sanae Takaichi’s statements about the Japanese military being able to come to Taiwan’s aid in case of a Chinese invasion attempt because US-Japanese-Taiwanese cooperation is crucial for defending the First Island Chain. The line of containment extends from Japan through Taiwan and the Philippines to Borneo. This chain forms the primary barrier restricting the Chinese Navy’s access to the western Pacific. Control of Taiwan would allow the Chinese Navy (PLAN) to bypass the chokepoints that U.S. and allied forces currently dominate (Miyako Strait, Bashi Channel, Luzon Strait), effectively breaking the First Island Chain and turning the East and South China Seas into zones of Chinese maritime dominance. The concept of the “island chains” was first articulated in 1951 by U.S. Secretary of State John Foster Dulles during the negotiations for the San Francisco Peace Treaty with Japan. Dulles described the arc of islands stretching from the Aleutians to Southeast Asia as a strategic “offshore island chain” that the United States and its allies would organize and defend to contain the Soviet Union and Communist China. The framework was subsequently embedded in the 1951 U.S.-Japan Security Treaty, the 1954 Southeast Asia Collective Defense Treaty (Manila Pact, and related policy documents of the early Cold War period. If China would be able to break through the First Island Chain they would run into another with Guam as its strongpoint. The Second Island Chain runs approximately from central Japan through Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, and Palau to western New Guinea. It serves as the secondary line of defense and hosts major U.S. power-projection bases, particularly on Guam. By holding the Second Island Chain, the U.S. would still be able to compete with the Chinese Navy in the western Pacific. However, The Third Island Chain is all about being able to protect North America from a Chinese invasion of the PLAN would grow significantly in size in the future. It centers on the Hawaii and extends through Midway Atoll and U.S. territories in the central Pacific. If the PLAN breaks through the First Island Chain, it gains freedom of maneuver in the Philippine Sea, places the Second Island Chain under persistent anti-access/area-denial pressure, disrupts reinforcement of Japan, South Korea, and the Philippines, and ultimately threatens U.S. naval predominance across the Pacific. Contemporary U.S. policy documents, including the 2022 National Defense Strategy and the Taiwan Relations Act, continue to treat Taiwan’s position in the First Island Chain as a core strategic interest. However, in order to be able to defend Taiwan from a Chinese invasion or blockade, U.S. bases in Japan as well as direct aid in battle by Japan would be crucial. This is why the U.S. has been sending signals for many years now that they wound want to see a much larger Japanese military force, including its Navy. With the new PM, Japan could be about to speed up that process that started with PM Shinzo Abe more than 10 years ago. Sanae Takaichi has positioned herself as a “China Realist” and has made it clear that Japan won’t back down from a fight if Chinese aggression in the western Pacific will threaten Japan’s national security.
